plain: Makes a copy of the text with the first letter big and every other letter small.
Counts how many items in a list are the same as the value you hand it. A value that isn't there counts 0.
Reads a key gently. `hero.get("glug", 0)` gives the value, or 0 when the key is missing, with no KeyError.
Puts a new item into a list at a position: the position first, then the value. Every item after it moves one place along.
The dot means: ask this text to do something. `.lower()` gives a copy in small letters. The text in the box does not change.
Takes the last item off a list and hands it back. `.pop(0)` takes the first item instead. The list gets shorter.
Takes the first item that is the same as the value you hand it out of a list. You give the value, not the position. If the value isn't there, Python stops with a ValueError.
Joins two questions. `a and b` is `True` only when both are `True`.
Adds one item to the end of a list. It changes the list itself and hands back nothing.
The value you hand over when you call a recipe. In `warn("Lucky")`, the argument is `"Lucky"`.
A line that says what must be true. If it is true, nothing happens. If it is not, Python stops with `AssertionError`.
`>=` means *at least*: exactly the number still counts. `<=` means *at most*. `>` and `<` leave the number itself out.
Python's message when a dot asks for something that is not there. Read a dictionary with square brackets, not a dot: `lucky["mana"]`, not `lucky.mana`.
The indented lines under an `if`, `elif` or `else`. They run together, or not at all.
The marks `(` and `)`. They come in pairs too. `print` keeps what it shows between them.
One path through an `if` chain: the `if` part, one `elif` part, or the `else` part. Only one runs.
A slip in the code. A loud bug stops Python with a message. A quiet bug runs, but gives a wrong answer: print the values to find it.
Running a recipe: its name, then brackets. `say_steady()` runs the steps once. No brackets, no run.
One small task in an exercise. It turns green when your code does it.
The `:` mark at the end of an `if`, `elif` or `else` line. It says: here comes the block.
A line that starts with `#`. Python skips it. It is a note for people.
A yes/no question about two values, like `dex < needed`. The signs are `<` `>` `<=` `>=` `==` `!=`. Python answers `True` or `False`.
The space under the editor. Your printed lines and Python's messages show up there.
A number with a point in it, like `24.0` or `42.5`. Dividing with `/` always gives one.
The word that makes a recipe: `def`, the recipe's name, brackets, and a colon. The steps go under it, indented. `def` never makes a box.
Made already. A name is defined once a line like `name = value` has run. "Not defined" means Python looked for something saved with that name and found nothing.
Values kept under keys, in curly brackets. Each key, then a colon, then its value. Commas go between.
Short for else, if: another question, asked only when the ones above were `False`. Python takes the first branch whose answer is `True`.
The part that runs when the `if` question was `False`. It has no question of its own.
Python's note that it could not finish your code. It is information, not a mark. Read the last line first, then look at the line it names.
Divide, then keep only the whole part. `50 // 12` is 4, because 12 fits into 50 four whole times.
Join texts end to end with `+`. Python adds no spaces, so put the spaces inside the quotes.
A line that asks a yes-or-no question. When the answer is `True`, Python runs the indented lines under it. When it is `False`, Python skips them.
Brings in a set of tools Python keeps on the shelf. `import random` brings in Python's dice.
Asks whether a value is somewhere in a list. Python answers `True` or `False`.
Spaces at the start of a line. Four spaces under an `if` mean: this line belongs to the `if`.
An item's place in a list. Counting starts at 0, so `[0]` is the first item. `[-1]` counts from the end: the last item.
Python's message when you ask for a position the list doesn't have. A list of 7 items has positions 0 to 6, so `[7]` is out of range.
example: IndexError: list index out of range

plain: A command that asks a question and waits for an answer. The answer always comes back as text.
Turns text that looks like a whole number into a real number, so you can do math with it. `int("3")` gives 3.
`==` asks whether two values are the same. `!=` asks whether they are different. One `=` does something else: it puts a value in a box (read it as *gets*).
The tag on one value in a dictionary. A key is text, so it has quotes: `"mana"`. Read its value with the key in square brackets.
Python's message when a dictionary has no key spelled exactly like that. Check the spelling, the capitals and the spaces.
Counts the items in a list. The last position is always one less than `len()`, because counting starts at 0.
Many values kept under one name, in order. Square brackets hold the list, and commas go between the items.
A list whose items are lists, like rows on a shelf. Read the row first, then the item in it: `roster[3][1]`.
A list whose items are dictionaries. Pick a sheet by its position first, then read it by key.
Another way to choose: `match choice:` then one `case` for each value. `case _:` catches anything else.
example:
match choice:
    case "option 1":
        print("Then we leave at dawn.")
    case _:
        print("Hm.")

plain: The signs Python does math with: `+` adds, `-` subtracts, `*` multiplies (times), `/` divides.
`max()` hands back the biggest item in a list, and `min()` the smallest, wherever they are.
Python met a name that no line has made yet. Often a typo, a capital letter, missing quotes, or a box used before the line that makes it.
example:
print(mama)
NameError: name 'mama' is not defined

plain: A dictionary kept as a value inside another dictionary. Read it with two keys in a row: the outer key first, then the inner key.
Python's word for nothing. A recipe with no `return` line hands back `None`.
Flips a yes-or-no answer. `not True` is `False`, and `not False` is `True`.
`in` asks whether a key is in a dictionary, and gives `True` or `False`. `not in` asks whether it is missing. Both look at the keys only, never the values.
A value Python can do math with. Numbers have no quotes: `3` is a number, `"3"` is text.
Joins two questions. `a or b` is `True` when at least one of them is `True`.
The order Python does math in. Brackets first, then `**`, then `*` `/` `//` `%`, then `+` and `-`. So `2 + 3 * 4` is 14.
What your program shows on the screen when it runs.
Two lists kept in step: item 0 of one goes with item 0 of the other, and so on. Change one, and you must change the other the same way.
An ingredient's name on the recipe card, in the brackets on the `def` line. It is a box that gets filled each time the recipe is called.
A line that does nothing. A recipe needs at least one line inside it, so `pass` holds the spot, like a blank recipe card, until you write a real step.
A stand-in value, like the `0` in a starter. It holds the place until you put the real thing there.
A number times itself, again and again. `2 ** 3` means 2 × 2 × 2, which is 8.
The Python command that shows words on the screen, in the console.
The question `input()` shows before it waits, like `"Who goes there? "`.
The marks around words: `"` or `'`. They come in pairs, one before the words and one after.
`random.randint(1, 6)` gives a random whole number from 1 to 6. Both ends are included.
Counts from a start number up to a stop number. The stop is left out: `range(1, 7)` gives 1 to 6. `list(range(1, 7))` turns the count into a list.
A named set of steps, made with `def`. Making a recipe does not run it. Calling its name with `()` runs the steps. Python calls a recipe a function.
What is left over after dividing. `50 % 12` is 2: four 12s make 48, and 2 is left.
Hands a value back to the line that called the recipe, and ends the recipe. Catch it in a box, or it is gone: `lucky_max = max_mana_for(13)`.
Tell Python to do your lines, from top to bottom. Press Run as often as you like. It costs nothing.
Build a value from boxes, like `total_cost = lantern_cost + rope_cost`, instead of typing the answer. Then it stays right when a box changes.
A copy of part of a list, made with a colon: `[2:5]` takes positions 2, 3 and 4. The end is left out. The list itself does not change.
`sorted(wall)` hands back a new list, smallest first, and leaves `wall` as it is. `wall.sort()` sorts the list itself and hands back nothing.
`*` with text and a number stamps the text that many times. `"█" * 3` gives `███`.
Turns a value into text. `str(26)` gives the text `"26"`, which can be glued to other text.
Words inside quotes. Python shows them exactly as you typed them.
Adds up every number in a list and hands back the total.
Python could not read a line: a missing quote, bracket or colon, or a sign it does not know. Nothing runs until it is mended.
Python's full message when a program stops. Read the last line first: the error's name, then what went wrong. Above it, the message names the line where Python stopped.
example:
File "main.py", line 4
NameError: name 'mana_cost' is not defined

plain: Three quote marks in a row, `"""`. The text between two sets of them can run over many lines.
Python's yes and no. They have capital letters and no quotes. A question like `6 > 15` gives back one of them.
Like a list that can't change. Round brackets instead of square ones. You read it by position, like a list, but you can't add, remove or swap its items.
Two values that don't fit together, like text glued to a number. Turn the number into text with `str()`, or take the quotes off a number.
example:
print("Mana: " + 7)
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

plain: The thing inside a box: text in quotes, like `"Lucky"`, or a number, like `26`.
The value is the right kind, but Python can't use it here. With a list, often `.remove()` of a value that is not in it.
example:
[48, 47].remove(99)
ValueError: list.remove(x): x not in list

plain: A box with a label. The label is the name. Inside is a value. You make one with `name = value`.
Pairs up two lists, item by item: first with first, second with second. Each pair is a tuple. Wrap it in `list()` to see the pairs.
